content: Sulfapyridine, also historically spelled as sulphapyridine in the UK, is a sulfonamide antibacterial agent. It was once commonly referred to as M & B. However, it is no longer prescribed for the treatment of infections in humans. Despite this, it may still be used in the management of linear IgA disease. While sulfapyridine is an effective antibacterial drug, its water solubility is highly dependent on pH levels. This characteristic poses a risk of crystallization within the bladder or urethra, potentially causing pain or obstruction. Like other sulfonamides, sulfapyridine carries a significant risk of agranulocytosis, a serious condition involving a dangerously low number of white blood cells. This risk, rather than the development of bacterial resistance, is the primary reason for its decline in medical use. Sulfapyridine was discovered by Lionel Whitby at the British pharmaceutical company May & Baker Ltd. It was first recorded in their Test Book on November 2, 1937, under the code name M & B 693. The drug gained historical significance when it was successfully used to treat Winston Churchill's bacterial pneumonia in 1942. Churchill later praised the drug in a radio broadcast, stating, This admirable M & B, from which I did not suffer any inconvenience, was used at the earliest moment and, after a week's fever, the intruders were repulsed. In 1944, M & B 693 also saved Nero, a lion from the Royal Circus, from pneumonia. The drug sulfasalazine is structurally composed of one molecule of mesalamine linked to one molecule of sulfapyridine via an azo bond. M & B 693 was among the first generation of sulfonamide antibiotics and has been reported as the first chemical cure for pneumonia. It could be administered either in tablet form or as a powder applied directly to wounds. During the Second World War, sulfapyridine was used so extensively that May & Baker struggled to meet the high demand. However, it was eventually largely replaced by penicillin and other sulfonamides.
